findings.paper_title: CIL Joint Committee Decisions from the 13th July 2026 Meeting
findings.headline: Unitary authority restructuring creates unresolved legal and financial implications for CIL Joint Committee
findings.detail: Gloucestershire was confirmed on 16 July 2026 to become a single unitary authority. The Structural Changes Order enabling this restructuring had not yet been made at report date. Legal and financial implications for CIL Joint Committee arrangements remain unaddressed pending the Orders.
findings.matters: Institutional restructuring creates uncertainty about continuation of joint CIL pooling arrangements and management of financial commitments through transition period
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: With the Local Government Reorganisation decision on 16 July 2026 confirming that Gloucestershire will become a single unitary authority this may have implications as the district council progresses through the transitional stage

findings.paper_title: CIL Joint Committee Decisions from the 13th July 2026 Meeting
findings.headline: M5 Junction 10 scheme: CIL receipts recalled from GCoC after original delivery phase funding purpose could no longer be met
findings.detail: The council sought approval to enforce against the original M5 Junction 10 CIL grant funding agreement because receipts paid to Gloucestershire County Council can no longer be used for their originally-allocated purpose. Approximately £1.029m is being returned to Gloucester while remaining allocated to the project but now for construction phase instead of delivery phase. This required execution of a replacement CIL grant funding agreement.
findings.matters: Enforcement of funding agreement and phase-shifting of deployment suggests either project scope changes, timeline revisions, or issues with original delivery structure that affect committed infrastructure spending
findings.figures: £1,029,000 returned to Gloucester; £244,272 Gloucester's share of current allocation; up to £20m additional to project
findings.quote: as the CIL receipts paid to Gloucestershire County Council (GCoC), can no longer be used by it for the purpose they were allocated for, agreeing that they remain allocated to the project to be spend on the construction phase of the project instead

findings.headline: Grant payment schedules being reprofiled for both M5 Junction 10 and Bus Rapid Transit schemes
findings.detail: The M5 Junction 10 scheme funding agreement is based on reprofiled grant requirements, and the Bus Rapid Transit scheme is undergoing a variation to enable reprofiling of grant payments. Reprofiling indicates delays to both capital projects.
findings.matters: Capital project delays signal execution risk and suggest the council's delivery track record may extend further, with knock-on effects on infrastructure progress and potential for additional financing needs
findings.figures: Not itemised
findings.quote: enter into a new funding agreement, based on reprofiled grant requirements, with Gloucestershire County Council. APPROVE the entering into of a variation of the Bus Rapid Transit (previously named Mass Rapid Transit) CIL grant funding agreement dated 23 April 2026 to enable a reprofiling of grant payments

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 CIL Joint Committee 13 July 2026 Decisions
findings.headline: Committee conditions further CIL allocation on CIL income reaching projected levels within M5 scheme delivery timescale
findings.detail: The decision includes a contingency clause stating that if the 75% portion of the Infrastructure Fund does not reach anticipated levels within the M5 Junction 10 project delivery timescale, further reconsideration will be given to funds ringfenced for local strategic infrastructure projects. This hedging language indicates uncertainty about CIL income forecasts.
findings.matters: The council itself acknowledges CIL income may fall short of the levels underpinning the £20m commitment, indicating forecast risk and potential funding gaps for infrastructure delivery
findings.figures: 75% portion of Infrastructure Fund
findings.quote: should the 75% portion of the Infrastructure Fund not reach the anticipated levels within the report within the M5 Junction 10 scheme project delivery timescale, further consideration be given as regards the portion of Infrastructure Fund currently ringfenced for allocation to local strategic infrastructure projects

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 CIL Joint Committee 13 July 2026 Decisions
findings.headline: £2.9m allocated plus up to £20m future CIL income ringfenced for single M5 Junction 10 scheme
findings.detail: Unallocated CIL receipts of £2,924,699 have been allocated to M5 Junction 10, with future CIL income within the 75% portion of the Infrastructure Fund ringfenced for the same scheme up to a maximum of £20m. This concentrates a large portion of infrastructure capital into a single project.
findings.matters: Committing over £20m to a single scheme represents concentration risk; if the scheme stalls, costs escalate, or CIL income underperforms, the council has constrained flexibility to fund other infrastructure priorities
findings.figures: £2,924,699 allocated; £20m maximum future allocation

findings.headline: The s106/DFG grants scheme has overspent its budget by £100,970 in the first quarter, but the forecast remains at budget.
findings.detail: The scheme was budgeted at £110,000 for 2026-27 but has spent £210,970 by end of June, a 92% overspend. Despite this significant early variance, the full-year forecast remains at the original £110,000, unchanged from the April budget projection.
findings.matters: A budget line overshooting by nearly its full value in Q1, with no corresponding forecast revision, suggests either poor budget setting or forecasts that are not responsive to early-period performance. For a lender, this indicates real budget discipline risk; for the finance director, it suggests monitoring controls may need tightening.
findings.figures: Budget £110,000; Actual Apr-Jun 26 £210,970; Variance (£100,970); Full-year forecast £110,000
findings.quote: Other Grant Funded Schemes - s106/DFG 110,000         210,970      (100,970)       110,000

findings.headline: Over half of Gloucester's borrowing is due to mature within 12 months, creating significant refinancing needs
findings.detail: The maturity structure shows 54.47% of the council's fixed and variable rate borrowing matures within 12 months, with a further 20.30% due in 12–24 months. This front-loaded maturity profile means the council faces substantial debt refinancing in 2026/27, representing both a cash flow need and market access requirement.
findings.matters: Refinancing risk is material to lenders assessing the council's debt sustainability and market exposure, and to the finance director's cash management and borrowing planning for the coming financial year.
findings.figures: 54.47% due in under 12 months; 20.30% due in 12–24 months; gross external debt £262.505m (within £305m prudential limit)
findings.quote: Under 12 months 0% - 100% 54.47%

findings.headline: Gloucester is using short-term borrowing to finance the Forum capital project, planning to restructure when construction completes.
findings.detail: The council deliberately chose short-term borrowing for capital funding rather than long-term PWLB borrowing, because short-term rates are currently lower than long-term rates. They acknowledge this is temporary funding for the Forum project and will restructure the borrowing once the asset is complete, in consultation with treasury advisors.
findings.matters: The strategy creates refinancing risk: the council must successfully re-finance short-term debt at acceptable rates when the Forum completes, and the timing coincides with an environment where rate cuts are now unlikely for an extended period.
findings.figures: Short-term investment return 3.25%, Bank Rate fell from 4.50% to 3.75% through 2025/26 but market outlook has shifted; £4.290m in investments at year-end
findings.quote: The council have taken the decision to borrow short term to fund the Capital Programme, short-term rates are lower than long term due to the Normal Guilt curve we are experiencing. As the Forum is still under construction we are able to absorb these financing costs and spread them over the life of the asset. Once the asset is complete we will make a decision, alongside our advisors, on the best way to structure our borrowing.

findings.headline: Cemeteries and Crematorium service forecast £188k overspend with rising maintenance costs and declining income
findings.detail: The service is experiencing increased costs for buildings and grounds maintenance, with further cremator repair works required. Income is declining due to lower cremation and memorial fees, reflecting post-Covid market changes including shift to direct cremations. Replacement of one cremator is due to start in September and could further impact income.
findings.matters: Essential service experiencing margin compression; capital-dependent infrastructure facing replacement costs; income under pressure from market changes; adds to cash pressure.
findings.figures: £188k forecast overspend; cremation income declining post-Covid; cremator replacement works imminent
findings.quote: The works to replace the cremators is due to start in September which could impact on income although measures have been put in place to try and minimise any impact on cremations throughput.

findings.headline: Council received £15.5m Exceptional Financial Support from MHCLG over 2024-27, signalling government recognition of financial distress
findings.detail: The council received EFS approval in February 2026 totalling £15.5m across three years. This was conditional on submission of a recovery plan, which is being monitored internally. An external assurance review was also completed with recommendations that require ongoing monitoring and reporting.
findings.matters: EFS indicates the council was already in recognized financial difficulty; recovery is conditional and externally supervised; lender needs to monitor whether recovery plan targets are being met.
findings.figures: £15.5m EFS approved; spread across 2024-25, 2025-26 and 2026-27
findings.quote: An application for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) was approved by the MHCLG in February 2026 for £15.5m over three years 2024-25, 2025-26 & 2026-27.

findings.headline: Interest rate risk on short-term borrowing creating £420k forecast overspend with volatility exposure
findings.detail: The council's borrowing is heavily weighted to short-term agreements in a high interest rate environment. Interest costs are forecast £420k over budget due to economic uncertainty and volatile rates. This is explicitly identified as a significant risk. Interest income partially mitigates the impact but remains volatile.
findings.matters: Short-term borrowing in volatile rate environment increases debt servicing costs unpredictably; refinancing risk as rates remain elevated; limits financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £420k interest cost overspend forecast; interest income benefit of £181k only partially offsets
findings.quote: The interest on borrowing remains a significant risk due to the amount of borrowing on short term agreements and the volatility of interest rates.

findings.headline: Council holds no general fund reserves, creating critical vulnerability to any adverse variance or unplanned cost
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it does not hold general fund reserves to deal with unplanned variances, making accurate forecasting and tight budgetary control essential. This position leaves the council with no financial buffer should any significant variance materialize.
findings.matters: Zero reserves is a critical stability risk for any local authority; any adverse variance in the major budget pressures (parking, property, interest costs) cannot be absorbed and would immediately require emergency action or additional borrowing.
findings.figures: £0 general fund reserves
findings.quote: This Council does not have any general fund reserves to deal with unplanned variances and as such accurate forecasting and tightly controlled budgets is essential.

findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio forecast £530k overspend driven by retail estate weakness and high vacant service charges
findings.detail: The council's city-centre retail property portfolio is suffering from general tenant turnover at Eastgate and Kings Walk shopping centres, which impacts income. Void properties add service charge costs. The newly completed Forum development has vacant space with service charges being picked up by the council as landlord. The council must actively manage properties to avoid further losses.
findings.matters: Underperforming regeneration investments reduce available cash; retail market exposure signals revenue volatility; council is absorbing landlord costs for vacant space.
findings.figures: £530k forecast overspend; £1.7m net income budget reduction made in 2025 to reflect current activity and costs
findings.quote: At Eastgate and Kings walk shopping centre a general tenant turnover has impacted on income, void properties also add service charge costs and other costs so proactively managing these properties is essential.

findings.headline: Parking service forecast £768k over budget with loss-making new Forum car park and contractual cost underestimation
findings.detail: The costs budget is understated by approximately £360k for contractual commitments (enforcement, ticket machine maintenance) that were not reflected in budgets. The new Forum car park has become operational but is forecasting losses due to high service charges (£200k per annum) and low usage. Discussions are ongoing to understand the position and improve where possible, but no solution is in place.
findings.matters: A £768k overspend on an essential service with no clear recovery plan signals operational management challenges and cash pressure; this comes after a £387k overspend in 2025-26.
findings.figures: £768k forecast overspend; £360k contractual costs underestimated; £200k annual service charge for Forum car park
findings.quote: The forecast for this year if the issues are not addressed is for the service to be over budget by £768K.

findings.headline: Council using short-term borrowing to fund Forum capital project, deferring long-term refinancing decision
findings.detail: The council did not undertake new long-term PWLB borrowing in 2025/26, instead choosing to use short-term borrowing to fund the capital programme while the Forum is under construction, because short-term rates are currently lower than long-term rates. The council will make a long-term borrowing decision once the Forum is complete, and will spread financing costs over the asset life.
findings.matters: This approach creates a future refinancing event. When the Forum is complete, the council will need to refinance or convert the short-term borrowing to long-term funding, potentially at higher rates if the inflation and rate-rise risks mentioned in the interest rate outlook materialise.
findings.figures: Specific Forum borrowing amounts not disclosed. Bank Rate fell 0.75% during the year (from 4.50% to 3.75%). Outlook notes commentators anticipate rates may not be cut further and could increase due to inflation pressures.
findings.quote: The council have taken the decision to borrow short term to fund the Capital Programme, short-term rates are lower than long term due to the Normal Guilt curve we are experiencing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - IA Activity Progress Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Management of public open spaces audit reveals weak performance monitoring and data governance controls
findings.detail: Audit gave 'Acceptable' assurance but identified gaps: KPIs are high-level and not measurable; no consistent process for logging service requests; tree management system lacks identifier to distinguish emergency from routine works; asset register is not regularly cleansed. Weaknesses in version control and staff resilience noted.
findings.matters: Weak performance monitoring and data governance in asset management create risk of service failures, unreliable reporting, and poor prioritization of work—factors that could affect service quality and cost control.
findings.figures: 2 medium-priority recommendations; 3 low-priority recommendations
findings.quote: KPIs are high-level and are not defined in a quantifiable or measurable manner, not covering internal operational performance; There is a lack of consistent guidance and processes around the reporting and logging of service requests.

findings.headline: 11 live fraud investigations underway as of August 2026, plus 38 National Fraud Initiative matches pending investigation
findings.detail: Counter Fraud Team closed 10 investigations in the first 4 months of 2026–27. Currently managing 11 live investigations, some jointly with DWP. NFI data-matching exercise has identified 38 potential fraud or error cases, primarily in Single Person Discount and council tax areas, requiring further assessment.
findings.matters: Active fraud investigations indicate financial risk. NFI matches suggest potential errors or losses in council-managed benefits or tax systems, which could affect net financial position.
findings.figures: 10 closed investigations; 11 live investigations; 38 NFI matches under investigation
findings.quote: As of 10 August 2026, the CFT has closed 10 investigations relating to Gloucester City Council during the current financial year. There are currently 11 live investigations relating to Gloucester City Council.

findings.headline: Underlying budget shows a deficit of £0.6m even before accounting adjustments
findings.detail: The Expenditure and Funding Analysis shows a deficit of £0.6m for the year, indicating the Council's spending exceeded its revenues. This reflects an ongoing structural imbalance in the budget.
findings.matters: A deficit in the primary funding analysis means the Council's operations are not sustainable from its own revenues and require ongoing external support to avoid escalating reserves depletion.
findings.figures: £0.6m deficit in 2025/26
findings.quote: It shows there was a deficit for the year of £0.6m.

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves have fallen to £1.188m and are continuing to decline
findings.detail: The Council's only remaining financial reserves are earmarked reserves totalling £1.188m. These are explicitly noted as reducing, leaving minimal financial cushion for a city council.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves indicate the Council cannot sustain operations from revenue and must draw down capital reserves, leaving no buffer for unexpected pressures or unfunded liabilities.
findings.figures: £1.188m earmarked reserves (declining)
findings.quote: The Council still holds earmarked reserves of £1.188m but this is reducing.

findings.headline: The Council has no general fund balances and required £15.5m Exceptional Financial Support to balance its accounts
findings.detail: Gloucester has zero general fund balances. To present balanced accounts, the Council applied for Exceptional Financial Support from the Government totalling £15.5m across three financial years. Of this, £4.28m was drawn down in 2025/26. EFS is reserved for councils in genuine financial difficulty and requires a recovery plan to restore sustainable finances.
findings.matters: A council with no general fund balances has no financial flexibility whatsoever and complete dependence on government support indicates severe structural distress.
findings.figures: £0 general fund balances; £15.5m total EFS; £4.28m EFS used in 2025/26
findings.quote: The Council has no general fund balances, the only option to present a balanced set of accounts was to apply for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from the Government. The application for EFS was £15.5m in total covering three financial years. The EFS used in 2025/26 was £4.28m.

findings.headline: Prior internal audit plans inadequate; governance weakness in audit oversight and risk coverage
findings.detail: Auditor identified that previous Internal Audit plans did not provide adequate coverage of key financial system risks. Documented as significant value-for-money weakness affecting governance and efficiency. Recommendations made October 2025.
findings.matters: Weak internal audit means management lacks independent assurance over controls; indicates governance failure and increases likelihood of undetected financial risk.
findings.figures: Statutory recommendations issued 30 October 2025
findings.quote: Inadequate internal audit coverage of key financial system risks, in the presence of fundamental weaknesses in the internal control framework, limits the Council's ability to manage financial risks effectively and weakens financial governance and oversight.

findings.headline: IFRS 16 leases not audited in 2024/25; £41.4m in lease assets and liabilities at risk
findings.detail: IFRS 16 introduced 1 April 2024 but not audited in 2024/25. 2025/26 is second year of application. Current balances: £9.8m right-of-use assets and £31.6m lease liabilities. Risk of incomplete lease identification and incorrect measurement.
findings.matters: Lease accounting is complex; absence of prior audit creates systemic misstatement risk affecting both assets and liabilities simultaneously.
findings.figures: Right-of-use assets: £9.8m; Lease liabilities: £31.6m at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: Right to use asset: £9.8 million; Lease liabilities 31.6 million.

findings.headline: Large property portfolio (£345m) revalued under new CIPFA Bulletin 22; increased valuation estimation risk
findings.detail: Council holds £275m PPE (£197m land/buildings) and £69.9m investment property. 2025/26 introduces mandatory quinquennial revaluation or five-year rolling programme under CIPFA Bulletin 22. Risk of understatement or incorrect posting of valuations.
findings.matters: Large asset base means valuation errors could be material to balance sheet; new revaluation regime introduces judgement risk and complexity.
findings.figures: PPE total: £275m; Land and buildings: £197m; Investment Property: £69.9m
findings.quote: Property, plant and equipment: £275 million; Relating to land and buildings: £197 million; Investment Property: £69.9m

findings.headline: Material pension liability of £21.9m; first audit post-2025 triennial valuation at risk of estimation error
findings.detail: Council's net pension liability is £21.9m, a material balance. 2025/26 is first year following 2025 triennial revaluation. Auditor will engage specialists to review actuarial assumptions and pension fund membership data, including asset ceiling calculations.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities materially affect balance sheet; underestimation hides true financial burden; actuarial assumptions are inherently uncertain.
findings.figures: Net pension liability: £21.9 million at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026 the Council's net pension liability totalled £21.9 million

findings.headline: Auditor will not rebuild assurance over historic reserves in 2025/26; recovery to qualified opinion delayed
findings.detail: Because planned audit procedures were not completed in 2023/24 and 2024/25, the auditor will NOT rebuild assurance over the historic position during 2025/26. Only in-year 2025/26 procedures are planned. Recovery timeline to qualified or unmodified opinion extends beyond this year.
findings.matters: Delayed recovery from disclaimed opinion means prior-year balances remain unaudited; opening balances for 2025/26 are at risk of undetected error.
findings.figures: Risk assessment completed 30 June 2026; recovery per NAO LARRIG 01 guidance
findings.quote: However, because we were unable to complete all planned audit procedures for 2023/24 and 2024/25 for the reasons outlined above, we will not commence any rebuilding of assurance over the historic position during the 2025/26 audit cycle.

findings.headline: Ongoing impact of December 2021 cyber-attack remains identified as significant weakness
findings.detail: Cyber-attack impact continues to be identified as evidence of significant weaknesses in financial sustainability, governance, and efficiency. Council operated manual records for 14 months then hybrid systems for 13 months. Auditor will review business continuity arrangements.
findings.matters: Extended recovery from cyber-attack indicates weak IT resilience and operational controls; ongoing impact suggests systemic weaknesses in data integrity.
findings.figures: Manual operations: 20 Dec 2021–28 Feb 2023 (14 months); Hybrid: 1 March 2023–18 April 2024 (13 months)
findings.quote: Following the cyber-attack incident, the Council maintained manual records from 20 December 2021 to 28 February 2023 and then operated a hybrid process involving both manual and system-based records from 1 March 2023 to 18 April 2024.

findings.headline: Fundamental controls missing: no monthly control account or bank reconciliations in 2025/26
findings.detail: Council did not operate monthly control account reconciliations or monthly bank reconciliations during 2025/26. Auditor identifies this as a fraud risk because absence of these controls increases error risk and affects financial statement preparation.
findings.matters: Missing basic reconciliation controls create significant undetected error risk in general ledger and cash; indicates weak control environment throughout the entity.
findings.figures: Cyber impact: 20 Dec 2021–28 Feb 2023 manual records; 1 March 2023–18 April 2024 hybrid process
findings.quote: In addition, the Council did not operate a number of fundamental internal controls during 2025/26 including monthly control account reconciliations and the preparation of monthly bank reconciliations. The absence of control account reconciliations increases the risk of error during the year and affects the preparation of the financial statements.

findings.headline: Council not adequately prepared for audit; finance team lacks capacity and availability
findings.detail: Auditor concluded the Council was not adequately prepared for the 2025/26 audit. Specific issues: working papers not provided per agreed schedule, key finance personnel unavailable. Statutory recommendations issued recommending urgent review of finance team capacity and capability.
findings.matters: Inability to staff finance function undermines reporting accuracy and cash flow forecasting; delays audit completion and signals operational strain.
findings.figures: Statutory recommendations issued 30 October 2025
findings.quote: Based on our initial planning work for 2025/26, we concluded that the Council was not adequately prepared for the audit and that a number of improvements were required: The provision of working papers in line with the agreed Client Assistance Schedule and timetable. The availability of key finance personnel to support the phase of the audit in accordance with the agreed project plan.

findings.headline: Auditor expects to continue reporting adverse value-for-money on financial sustainability
findings.detail: Auditor made statutory recommendations in October 2025 on budget assumptions and monitoring. Based on current understanding, the auditor considers it likely to report by exception in 2025/26 on budgetary control and financial sustainability.
findings.matters: Adverse auditor comments on value-for-money are formal warnings about the council's ability to plan and manage resources; treated seriously by lenders and regulators.
findings.figures: Statutory recommendations issued 30 October 2025
findings.quote: The prior year significant weakness is an indicator of a risk in the current year. Based on our current understanding we consider it likely we will continue to report by exception in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Council received Exceptional Financial Support and depleted all usable reserves
findings.detail: Weaknesses in financial monitoring resulted in depletion of all usable reserves and emergence of negative general fund reserve position. The Council required Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from Central Government in 2025/26 to address the budget gap.
findings.matters: Loss of reserves and need for government bailout indicates severe financial distress and inability to service debt independently; critical for any lender assessment.
findings.figures: Materiality set at £0.922m (1% of £92m gross expenditure); EFS received 2025/26
findings.quote: Weaknesses in financial monitoring and reporting processes has a significant adverse financial impact on the Council, resulting in the depletion of all usable reserves, the emergence of a negative general fund reserve position, and an inability to set a balanced budget. As a consequence, the Council is required to seek Exceptional Financial Support from Government

findings.headline: Statutory recommendations issued in October 2025 for failure to prepare compliant financial statements and budgets
findings.detail: EY issued statutory recommendations because the council failed to prepare financial statements in accordance with statutory requirements and to set a budget based on an accurate financial position. EY identified this as a significant weakness in the council's arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness, and cited inadequate forecasting of reserves, limited finance team capacity, and late financial statement preparation.
findings.matters: Statutory recommendations indicate the council was not meeting legal obligations for financial governance. These deficiencies directly affect a lender's confidence in management capability and financial control.
findings.figures: Statutory recommendations issued October 2025
findings.quote: We issued statutory recommendations in October 2025 because the Council failed to prepare financial statements in accordance with statutory requirements or to set a budget based on an accurate financial position.

findings.headline: Auditor will deprioritize Gloucester in 2025/26 because it cannot support basic audit procedures
findings.detail: EY explicitly states it will focus audit resources on councils that have demonstrated they can adequately support completion of all planned 2025/26 audit procedures. The council was unable to support completion of all planned procedures through to 2024/25. EY will only reperform its risk assessment in 2026/27 to reassess whether the council can proceed with historical rebuild.
findings.matters: This signals the auditor has lost confidence in the council's capacity to meet basic audit requirements. Deprioritization means limited audit oversight of 2025/26 accounts and continued delay in assurance rebuilding, extending the period of unverified positions.
findings.figures: Risk reperformance planned for 2026/27 audit; rebuild decision deferred
findings.quote: we will therefore focus our audit resources on rebuilding assurance for those bodies that have demonstrated they are able to adequately support the completion of all 2025/26 planned audit procedures

findings.headline: Fundamental internal controls were not operated during 2024/25
findings.detail: The council did not operate monthly control account reconciliations or monthly bank reconciliations during 2024/25. This follows a cyber-attack incident that forced manual record-keeping from December 2021 to February 2023, then hybrid manual/system processes through April 2024. The absence of basic reconciliation controls significantly increases the risk of error in reported balances.
findings.matters: Monthly reconciliations are foundational controls; their absence creates direct risk that material errors in cash and account balances are undetected, affecting the reliability of financial reporting and cash flow visibility.
findings.figures: Manual records from 20 December 2021 to 28 February 2023; hybrid processes from 1 March 2023 to 18 April 2024; fundamental controls absent in 2024/25
findings.quote: the Council did not operate a number of fundamental internal controls during 2024/25, including monthly control account reconciliations and the preparation of monthly bank reconciliations.

findings.headline: Four consecutive years of disclaimed audit opinions with no rebuild commenced
findings.detail: Gloucester has received disclaimer opinions for 2021/22 through 2024/25, meaning the auditor could not form an opinion on the financial statements for that entire period. EY states that planned procedures to rebuild assurance could not be completed in either 2023/24 or 2024/25, so the natural rebuild process has yet to commence. This means reserve balances across four years remain unaudited.
findings.matters: An unaudited financial position for four years creates fundamental uncertainty about the council's actual financial standing, making it impossible for a lender to verify reserves, cash, or financial resilience.
findings.figures: Four years of disclaimer opinions (2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25); rebuild has not commenced as of the report date
findings.quote: planned procedures could not be completed in either 2023/24 or 2024/25. As a result, the 'natural' rebuild process to obtain assurance has yet to commence. This will be a priority focus for our 2025/26 audit.

findings.headline: Finance and Property Services were understaffed during 2025-26 and required additional capacity funding approved for 2026-27
findings.detail: Capacity issues were identified in Finance and Property Services during 2025-26, contributing to the financial management failures. The council approved additional funding in the 2026-27 budget to increase capacity and capability in these critical services. Interim support was also appointed to assist with preparing the 2024-25 and 2025-26 statement of accounts to meet statutory reporting deadlines.
findings.matters: Understaffing in finance functions during a year of financial difficulties directly contributed to the failure to monitor budgets and the discovery of the true position.
findings.figures: Additional funding approved for Finance and Property in 2026-27; interim support appointed for accounts closure
findings.quote: During 2025-26 capacity issues were identified in the Finance and Property Services. Additional funding was approved in the 2026-27 budget for increasing the capacity and capability in these services

findings.headline: Council has four consecutive years of disclaimed audit opinions (2021-22 to 2024-25) and only returned to normal audit timescales in 2025-26
findings.detail: The council has had disclaimed audits for four consecutive years due to both the national backlog and issues created by a cyber attack. The council has not published statutory accounts within the statutory deadline since 2020-21. The 2025-26 accounts are planned to be published on 30 June 2026, returning the council to normal timescales for the first time in six years. The external auditors plan to complete a full audit by the backlog deadline of 31 January 2027.
findings.matters: Four years of unsigned accounts prevents independent verification of the council's actual financial position and indicates sustained material weaknesses in financial reporting.
findings.figures: Disclaimed audits for 2021-22, 2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25; first on-time publication since 2020-21 planned for 30 June 2026
findings.quote: This Council has had disclaimed audits for 2021-22 to 2024-25. The plan is for the External Auditors to complete a full audit of the 2025-26 accounts before the backlog deadline 31st January 2027.

findings.headline: Council had no effective budget monitoring process during 2025-26, discovering the problem in September
findings.detail: During 2025-26, the council operated without a clear and robust budget monitoring process. This resulted in quarterly financial information presented to members not reflecting the correct outturn position, creating significant variances and drawing down reserves uncontrollably. A new budget monitoring process was only introduced in December 2025, mid-way through the financial year, in response to the discovery of these failures.
findings.matters: Absence of effective budget monitoring throughout a financial year means the council had no real-time visibility of its financial position or ability to manage variances.
findings.figures: Budget monitoring process introduced December 2025 (seven months into the financial year)
findings.quote: During 2025 it became apparent that there was not a clear and robust budget monitoring process in place and as such the quarterly financial information presented to Members did not reflect the correct outturn position leading to significant variations and impact on reserves.

findings.headline: Council explicitly failed to comply with CIPFA governance principles on financial management and internal control during 2025-26
findings.detail: The council states non-compliance with Principle D (determining interventions necessary to optimise outcomes) and Principle F (managing risks and performance through robust internal control). Both failures are attributed to 'lack of financial management and budgetary control'. The council acknowledges the budget monitoring process was not operating throughout 2025-26 and was only introduced in response to the financial issues discovered in September 2025.
findings.matters: Explicit non-compliance with core CIPFA governance principles indicates fundamental weaknesses in the council's control environment and financial stewardship.
findings.figures: Non-compliance in CIPFA Principles D and F
findings.quote: Principle D was not fully complied with due to the lack of financial management and budgetary control. Principle F was not fully complied with due to the lack of financial management and budgetary control.

findings.headline: External auditors issued three statutory recommendations in October 2025 due to financial management and internal control weaknesses
findings.detail: The external auditors formally issued three statutory recommendations to the council in October 2025. These were triggered by significant weaknesses in the council's budget monitoring process and the quality of financial information presented to members. The council states that external auditor findings and the Section 151 Officer's findings 'highlighted weaknesses with the financial management and reporting processes'. Progress against these recommendations is monitored by the Audit and Governance Committee.
findings.matters: Statutory audit recommendations represent material governance deficiencies that directly affect financial control and the reliability of council reporting.
findings.figures: Three statutory recommendations issued October 2025
findings.quote: In October 2025 the Council received three statutory recommendations from the auditors, these have been actioned and progress is monitored regularly by members of the AGC.

findings.headline: Council applied for £15.5m exceptional financial support after discovering budget monitoring failures had hidden the true financial position
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer identified significant financial management weaknesses in September 2025. These failures resulted in an application for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) of £15.5m covering 2024-25 to 2026-27. The original budget monitoring process was ineffective, causing quarterly financial information presented to members to not reflect the correct outturn position. To balance the 2026-27 budget, the council required this EFS plus £1m in additional reductions or income.
findings.matters: A £15.5m EFS application signals material financial distress and indicates the council's underlying position was worse than reported during the financial year.
findings.figures: £15.5m EFS covering 2024-25, 2025-26 and 2026-27; £1m in additional reductions/increased income required for 2026-27
findings.quote: application for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) for £15.5m covering 2024-25, 2025-26 and 2026-27

findings.headline: Major facilities management system decision deferred pending Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: The implementation of a CAFM (Computerized Facilities Management) system to track building maintenance, repairs and compliance is on hold. The September 2026 update states this decision must be reviewed in the context of LGR and whether it should be progressed before vesting day, creating ongoing uncertainty.
findings.matters: LGR (Local Government Reorganisation) creates structural uncertainty; decisions on major systems implementation directly affect service continuity and financial forecasting.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Management reporting is going to be difficult to manage until a decision has been made on the CAFM System this needs to be reviewed in the context of LGR and a decision on whether this should be progressed before vesting day.

findings.headline: £3 million planned capital spend on building works over two years
findings.detail: The Cultural Development Grants audit finding identified the need for a 10-year maintenance plan. The council now commits to spending £3 million on essential building works over the next two years, with the 10-year plan to be continually reviewed and updated.
findings.matters: Material capital commitments affect the council's borrowing position and cash flow forecasts; ongoing maintenance requirements indicate ageing asset portfolio.
findings.figures: £3 million over next 2 years
findings.quote: Over the next 2 years, a further £3 million will be spent on essential building works and the 10-year planned preventative maintenance plan will be continually reviewed and updated upon completion of the capital expenditure programme or if further works are required.

findings.headline: Three audit recommendations now overdue on implementation
findings.detail: The monitoring report lists three recommendations that have exceeded their implementation dates: Cultural Development Grants (target 29/05/26), Hempsted Meadow (target 07/11/25), and Freedom of Information (target 05/02/26). This indicates governance control issues are not being resolved on schedule.
findings.matters: Lenders care about audit findings being remediated promptly; unresolved audit recommendations indicate weaker internal controls and governance discipline.
findings.figures: Three recommendations overdue; FOI deadline 05/02/26, Hempsted Meadow 07/11/25, Cultural Development Grants 29/05/26
findings.quote:
Recommendation Monitoring - Recommendations Exceeded Implementation Date
Cultural Development Grants 29/05/26
Hempsted Meadow 07/11/25
Freedom of Information 05/02/26

findings.headline: Audit recommendations remain open from 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26, spanning up to three years
findings.detail: The report notes that recommendations from three prior financial years remain unimplemented. The specific details and remediation status are in Appendix B and the exempt Annex 1, but the continued carry-forward of recommendations from 2023-24 suggests some control issues identified three years ago have not yet been resolved.
findings.matters: A lender assesses a council's control environment and management response to identified weaknesses; recommendations open across multiple years indicate either control deficiencies or capacity constraints in remediation, both of which affect lending risk.
findings.figures: Open recommendations from 2023-24, 2024-25, 2025-26, and 2026-27
findings.quote: The number of recommendations that remain open from 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26, 2026-27 to date

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Internal Audit Progress Report
findings.headline: Financial Reconciliations and Controls audit delayed while finance team prioritizes Statutory Accounts
findings.detail: The Financial Reconciliations and Controls audit (high-risk) began fieldwork but has stalled. The finance team has had to reprioritize to focus on preparing Statutory Accounts, absorbing the capacity needed to progress this core audit. This is material because financial reconciliation controls are fundamental to a council's financial management.
findings.matters: A lender and finance director need confidence that core financial controls are being audited. A delay to this high-risk audit, driven by finance team capacity strain on statutory reporting, signals potential vulnerability in control oversight during the year.
findings.figures: High risk; fieldwork started but incomplete as of July 2026
findings.quote: Field work is in progress but has been delayed by the requirement for the Finance team to focus on the Statutory Accounts.

findings.headline: Capital programme is 36% underspent overall at mid-year
findings.detail: Of £58.7m budgeted for 2025-26, only £37.9m has been spent by December. At the halfway point, 64% of planned capital deployment has occurred with £20.8m remaining.
findings.matters: Significant capital programme slippage indicates the council may not deliver planned investment, requiring reforecasting and affecting growth and regeneration plans that support financial sustainability
findings.figures: Total budget £58,747,362, Actual spend £37,935,648, Underspent £20,811,713
findings.quote: TOTAL CAPITAL PROGRAMME 58,747,362  37,935,648  20,811,713

findings.headline: Three major schemes are 89–98% underspent: Leisure, Museum, Crematorium
findings.detail: Leisure Facilities (£8m budgeted, £878k spent), Museum Building Improvements (£2.4m budgeted, £149k spent), and Crematorium Cremator Improvements (£2.5m budgeted, £64k spent) show minimal deployment. Collectively these schemes are £24m behind budget.
findings.matters: Multiple major capital projects with minimal progress at mid-year indicates systemic delivery constraints or unrealistic budget planning that will affect the council's capital strategy
findings.figures: Leisure £8m budgeted vs £878k spent; Museum £2.4m budgeted vs £149k spent; Crematorium £2.5m budgeted vs £64k spent
findings.quote: Leisure Facilities Improvements 8,000,000  877,619  7,122,381; Museum Building Improvements 2,400,000  148,995  2,251,005; Crematorium Cremator Impovements 2,500,000  63,961  2,436,039

findings.headline: Greyfriars capital scheme is 97% underspent at mid-year
findings.detail: Greyfriars, budgeted at £12.2m for 2025-26, has spent only £422k by December. This major capital project has delivered less than 3% of its annual allocation in the first six months.
findings.matters: Minimal progress on a multi-million pound capital project raises questions about scheme viability, planning obstacles, or market conditions that could jeopardise capital programme delivery
findings.figures: Budget £12,200,000, Actual £422,048, Underspent £11,777,952

findings.headline: Kings Quarter is £6.3m over budget at mid-year
findings.detail: The Kings Quarter scheme budgeted at £18m for 2025-26 has already spent £24.3m by December, a 35% cost overrun in the first half of the year. This is the council's largest capital scheme by budget.
findings.matters: Major cost overruns on flagship regeneration projects signal delivery risk and suggest the full business case will be exceeded, directly affecting debt servicing capacity

findings.headline: Waste & Recycling overspent by £395k; Ubico contract performance and historical income loss
findings.detail: The council's largest service overspent by £395k. Part relates to loss of historical shared service income no longer received; the Ubico waste contract has minor pressures being managed. Bulky waste and garden waste performed better than expected.
findings.matters: Waste is typically a council's largest controllable spend. A £395k overspend on a £5.5m budget (7%) suggests either contract cost escalation or demand surge that the council cannot control.
findings.figures: Waste & Recycling £395k overspend on £5.511m budget
findings.quote: Waste & Recycling and Streetcare finished the year £276k over budget. The Ubico contract is regularly monitored and the main variances do not relate to overspend on the main Ubico contract, although there are some minor pressures which are being managed. The majority of the variance relates to a budget for an historical shared service income which is no longer received and was corrected in the 2026-27 budget.

findings.headline: Procurement Act 2023 delays cost £65k+ in lost leisure operator revenue for 2025-26
findings.detail: Freedom Leisure delays caused by new procurement rules have reduced expected revenue by £65k in 2025-26 and will impact 2026-27, with only partial offset from VAT changes.
findings.matters: Leisure revenues are key to many councils' income models. Procurement delays preventing capital works and delaying revenue recovery increase financial uncertainty.
findings.figures: £65k revenue shortfall in 2025-26; £40k shortfall remaining in 2026-27 after mitigation
findings.quote: the delay in these projects as a result of the lengthy procurement processes required under the Procurement Act 2023 have impacted on the expected revenue to be received from the operator in 2025-26 causing an adverse budget position of £65k

findings.headline: Capital programme severely underspent at £37.9m vs £54.8m budget; projects stalled in procurement
findings.detail: The council budgeted £54.8m for capital but only spent £37.9m. Leisure facilities, cremator works, and Greyfriars regeneration are all stalled in procurement processes, delaying £16.9m of planned investment.
findings.matters: Prolonged procurement delays and capital underspend suggest project delivery problems and may defer revenue streams (e.g., from leisure operator). It also indicates execution risk on regeneration plans that may be financing strategy.
findings.figures: £37.9m spent against £54.8m budget; £16.9m underspent
findings.quote: The Capital Programme for 2025-26 saw a spend of £37.9m against the budget for the year (including items carried forward from 2024-25) of £54.8m... The significant new items in the 2025-26 Capital budget (the leisure facilities, the cremator works, the Greyfriars regeneration project) are progressing through the relevant procurement processes and increased spend is expected once these have concluded and the works get underway.

findings.headline: Service closures and cuts: Blackfriars venue ceased operation, Museum hours reduced
findings.detail: As part of spending review for 2026-27, the council ceased operating Blackfriars venue from May 2026 and reduced Museum opening hours from April 2026. Festivals & Events funding was also reduced.
findings.matters: Service closures indicate the council is in contraction mode and cutting services to residents due to financial pressure, not strategic choice.
findings.figures: Blackfriars ceased May 2026; Museum hours reduced April 2026
findings.quote: The Blackfriars venue ceased to be operated by the Council from May 2026, and the Museum opening hours were reduced from April 2026. There will also be a reduction in the funding of Festivals & Events.

findings.headline: Major £951k variance between Q3 forecast and Q4 outturn shows forecasting unreliability
findings.detail: The council revised its Q3 forecast by £951k downward by year-end. Officers attribute this to budget monitoring only being in place since December with quality and timeliness issues in underlying data.
findings.matters: A £951k variance (33% of the final overspend) between quarters suggests the council cannot reliably predict its financial position, making budget assumptions unreliable.
findings.figures: £951k movement from Q3 forecast to Q4 outturn
findings.quote: The report highlights the movement between quarter 3 and final outturn which is a downward adjustment of £951k. This is a sizable variance but reflects that the budget monitoring had only been in place since December, so when the quarter 3 figures were produced, there were still issues with the quality and timeliness of the data, both of which are slowly improving.

findings.headline: Resources portfolio overspent by £1.612m, driven by commercial property void costs and tenant administration
findings.detail: The Resources portfolio is the worst performer. Commercial property saw £559k adverse variance due to higher service charge costs where tenants vacated, some entering administration. This suggests asset quality issues and non-performing investments.
findings.matters: Commercial property voids and tenant defaults indicate the council's property investments are underperforming and generating unexpected costs rather than income, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Resources portfolio £1.612m overspend; Commercial Property £559k adverse variance
findings.quote: Costs during Q4 have been higher than forecast as a result of the Council continuing to face higher service charge costs than budgeted where tenants have vacated properties, some at short notice due to entering administration.

findings.headline: External Auditors issued Statutory Recommendations in October 2025
findings.detail: The council faced serious enough governance and financial control issues that auditors formally escalated them via statutory recommendations. These led to unexpected additional costs for professional advice and audit fees.
findings.matters: Statutory recommendations indicate auditor concerns about financial control and governance. This is a formal escalation above routine management comments and signals control weaknesses.
findings.figures: £204k additional Financial & Corporate overspend related to professional advice and audit fees on these matters
findings.quote: This also reflects the issues raised in the External Auditors Statutory Recommendations issued in October 2025.

findings.headline: Year-end overspend of £1.125m despite £2.845m increase to base budgets
findings.detail: Members approved a permanent increase of £2.845m to base budgets in January 2026 to address identified budget pressures. Despite this, the council still finished the year £1.125m overspent against the revised budget.
findings.matters: The fact that a multi-million pound budget increase failed to prevent overspend suggests either structural demand problems or inability to control spending, both concerning for creditworthiness.
findings.figures: £2.845m budget increase approved; £1.125m year-end overspend recorded
findings.quote: Members approved a permanent increase to base budgets of £2.845m to address the identified budget pressures... The year-end position is a total overspend of £1,125k.

findings.headline: Council received £15.5m emergency government support because reserves fell negative
findings.detail: In 2024-25, overspends pushed the General Fund into a negative position. The council applied for and was approved for Exceptional Financial Support of £15.5m covering 2024/25, 2025/26 and 2026/27. This is emergency funding for a council unable to balance its accounts.
findings.matters: Negative reserves signal insolvency risk and government bailout is a critical red flag for any lender, as it indicates the council cannot manage its finances and has required state intervention.
findings.figures: £15.5m EFS approval for three-year period
findings.quote: the 2024-25 Statement of Accounts were completed and identified a further significant overspend, resulting in the Council's reserves falling into a negative position and leading to the submission of an Exceptional Financial Support application of £15.5m for 2024/25, 2025/26 & 2026/27, which has been approved.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Recommendation Monitoring Overdue Recommendations
findings.headline: Council relying on temporary contractors to establish basic property management systems and controls
findings.detail: To address repairs risk rating, management reporting, and periodic venue assessment, the council hired a temporary person on a 6-month contract starting 19 March 2026 who has experience in estate management systems. The council also notes that a new person is being employed to review and implement contractor control procedures. This suggests the council lacked in-house capacity to address basic asset management compliance.
findings.matters: Dependence on temporary contracts to implement basic governance and asset management controls suggests staffing constraints and potential knowledge gaps in property/asset management.
findings.figures: 6-month temporary contract starting 19 March 2026
findings.quote: A temporary person has been employed and starts on the 19th March who has experience in setting up and using the type of estate management systems that we required to report on these items more effectively.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Recommendation Monitoring Overdue Recommendations
findings.headline: Multiple audit recommendations on facilities, asset management, and debt controls remain unimplemented past deadlines with no management updates provided to audit committee
findings.detail: The document shows at least eight audit recommendations with implementation dates ranging from August 2024 to April 2026, nearly all marked "No management update received for this audit committee meeting." These cover facilities access controls, repairs risk rating, NNDR credit balance investigations, leaseholder performance monitoring, lease valuations, and debt recovery policy. This pattern suggests systematic delays in implementing audit actions.
findings.matters: Persistent failure to implement or report on audit recommendations indicates weak internal control governance and raises questions about whether audit findings are being taken seriously at operational level.
findings.figures: Approximately 8 recommendations with exceeded or approaching implementation dates
findings.quote: No management update received for this audit committee meeting

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Recommendation Monitoring Overdue Recommendations
findings.headline: Planned £3 million in essential building works over the next two years as part of compliance programme
findings.detail: Following a MEND grant audit, the council has committed to a 10-year planned preventative maintenance plan and will spend £3 million on essential building works over the next two years. The council is also instructing full stock condition surveys across its portfolio to create a 10-year planned maintenance schedule for each building.
findings.matters: A significant capital commitment signals either deferred maintenance backlog or condition issues in the council's property portfolio that require funded remediation.
findings.figures: £3 million over next 2 years
findings.quote: Over the next 2 years, a further £3 million will be spent on essential building works and the 10-year planned preventative maintenance plan will be continually reviewed and updated upon completion of the capital expenditure programme or if further works are required.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Recommendation Monitoring Overdue Recommendations
findings.headline: Health and safety audit recommendation from 2019 now significantly overdue with no management update
findings.detail: The council was instructed to clarify building manager responsibilities regarding premises H&S as part of a Limited Assurance audit in October 2023. The original target date was July 2019; it was revised to January 2026. The council's plan to implement this via a Techforge system was paused after a cyber incident due to lack of available resources. No management update has been received since the November 2023 relaunch meeting.
findings.matters: A seven-year-old H&S audit recommendation still unimplemented signals weak follow-through on audit actions and suggests resource or priority constraints affecting core property compliance.
findings.figures: Original target date 01/07/19, revised to 30/01/26
findings.quote: Following the Cyber incident and a lack of available resources, the project of implementing Techforge was paused. Property Services has relaunched the project and meetings have been agreed with Techforge in November 2023 to redesign the project plan.

findings.headline: Auditor issued statutory recommendations on finance team capacity and in-year financial monitoring processes
findings.detail: The auditor recommended urgent review of the finance team to ensure sufficient capacity and capability, a clear timetable for producing future accounts and AGS, and comprehensive review of in-year financial monitoring and reporting to ensure accuracy and support informed decision-making.
findings.matters: Statutory audit recommendations that question the finance team's capacity indicate the council lacks the capability to prepare accurate accounts or maintain effective financial control. This is a governance failure.
findings.figures: Three statutory recommendations issued on 30 October 2025
findings.quote: We recommend that the Council urgently review the Finance team to ensure that there is sufficient capacity and capability to support the breadth of its activities, including the preparation of accurate financial information to support informed decision making and to meet statutory reporting obligations.

findings.headline: Material accounting errors in pension liabilities and financial instruments; prior year figures remain unaudited
findings.detail: The auditor identified significant errors in the 2023/24 draft accounts including pension re-measurement corrections of £8.078m and £60.292m, overstated asset returns of £5.381m, and multiple misstatements in financial instrument disclosures. Prior year 2022/23 comparatives were also subject to disclaimed opinions and remain unaudited.
findings.matters: Large accounting corrections indicate weak financial reporting quality and increase the risk that material misstatement remains undetected. Unaudited prior years prevent reliable year-on-year comparison.
findings.figures: Pension error corrections: £8.078m (business combinations disposal), £60.292m (asset ceiling), £5.381m (return on assets overstated); pension re-measurement correction £8.078m
findings.quote: The CIES table includes a number of errors, specifically: The inclusion of the effect of business combinations and disposals of £8.078 million, which has been incorrectly presented; An asset ceiling adjustment of £-60.292 million has been incorrectly included

findings.headline: Council depleted all usable reserves and entered negative general fund reserve position; now dependent on government emergency funding
findings.detail: The council overspent its 2023/24 budget by £0.826 million (vs £0.288m initially reported), reducing reserves from £4.975m to £3.099m. In December 2025, council identified £4.3m overspend for 2024/25, resulting in negative general fund reserves of £3.89m. Unable to set balanced budget for 2025/26, council applied for and received Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) of £15.5 million in-principle from government.
findings.matters: A negative reserve position indicates the council cannot absorb unexpected costs or service demands. Dependency on emergency government funding signals financial distress and indicates the council cannot manage its finances sustainably.
findings.figures: 2023/24 overspend £0.826m; 2024/25 overspend £4.3m; negative reserves position £3.89m; EFS received £15.5m in-principle
findings.quote: In December 2025, the Council identified overspends of £4.3 million against the 2024/25 budget and a forecast overspend of £2.5 million against the 2025/26 budget. This resulted in the Council being in a negative general fund reserve position of £3.89 million for 2024/25.

findings.headline: Council lacks fundamental internal control framework: monthly reconciliations and budget monitoring not operating effectively
findings.detail: The council did not complete monthly control account reconciliations (including bank reconciliations) or maintain robust budget monitoring processes during 2023/24. The Council also operated hybrid manual and system-based records from March 2023 to April 2024 following the December 2021 cyber-attack, which the auditor identified as a significant risk of misstatement.
findings.matters: Absence of basic financial controls increases the risk of error, fraud, and misstatement in financial reporting. It limits oversight of resource use and the council's ability to manage its finances responsibly.
findings.figures: Manual records maintained 20 December 2021 to 28 February 2023; hybrid processes 1 March 2023 to 18 April 2024
findings.quote: The Council did not have an appropriate internal control framework to ensure that fundamental controls, such as: the completion of monthly control account reconciliations; the preparation of monthly bank reconciliations: and robust budget monitoring processes were operating effectively during 2023/24.

findings.headline: Auditor will issue a disclaimed audit opinion on the 2023/24 financial statements, meaning no assurance over the accounts
findings.detail: The auditor could not complete the necessary audit procedures due to the 28 February 2025 backstop date and delays in receiving draft accounts (published 8 September 2025, 16 months late). Combined with prior year disclaimers, this means no assurance over opening balances, in-year transactions, or closing balances.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the council's financial position is unaudited and unverified. Lenders and finance directors cannot rely on the accounts for decision-making.
findings.figures: Backstop date 28 February 2025; accounts published 8 September 2025, 16 months after statutory deadline of 31 May 2024
findings.quote: for the year ended 31 March 2024 we determined that we cannot meet the objectives of the ISAs(UK) and we anticipate issuing a disclaimed audit report.

findings.headline: Original governance statement revised following recent financial position concerns identified by auditors
findings.detail: The original AGS approved in July 2024 was updated after internal finance raised financial position concerns that featured in External Auditors Statutory Recommendations. The Head of Internal Audit and Section 151 Officer worked with external auditors on the revised final statement, which has been reviewed and amended.
findings.matters: External Auditor Statutory Recommendations signalling financial position concerns warrant formal revision of governance — indicates material issues requiring management attention and audit oversight
findings.quote: To provide a final AGS following the recent financial position highlighted by the internal finance team and included in the External Auditors Statutory Recommendations. This has been reviewed by the External Auditors and amendments are included.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing by £12.077m; net borrowing of £15.024m required in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council's cumulative debt (CFR) will increase by £12.077m during 2026/27 to reach £285.993m. Of the £22.603m capital programme, £15.024m will be financed through net borrowing (66% of total expenditure), with the remainder met from external grants (£4.169m), capital receipts (£1.2m), and revenue funding (£2.21m). This reliance on borrowing compounds existing high financing costs.
findings.matters: A lender tracks debt accumulation and borrowing requirements. The substantial CFR growth and high proportion of debt financing show the council is taking on material new debt commitments that will extend debt service obligations for decades, combining with existing revenue constraints.
findings.figures: CFR increase £12.077m, total CFR £285.993m, net financing need £15.024m, borrowing 66% of capital expenditure
findings.quote: The CFR is expected to increase by £12.077m during 2026/27.

findings.headline: Financing costs consume 37% of net revenue, indicating material debt burden and constrained financial flexibility
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs (interest and minimum revenue provision on debt) to net revenue stream stands at 37.17% in 2026/27, remaining at 37.27% in 2027/28 and 37.20% in 2028/29. This means over one-third of the council's available revenue is committed to debt service before any spending on services, significantly limiting the council's ability to respond to unexpected financial pressures or fund new initiatives.
findings.matters: A lender assessing creditworthiness must understand the council's revenue flexibility and debt burden. A financing costs ratio of 37% is materially high and indicates the council is heavily committed to historical borrowing decisions, constraining its capacity to absorb financial shocks.
findings.quote: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream 37.17%

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: Reserve levels inadequate and forecast to go negative without recovery plan delivery
findings.detail: The council's minimum prudent reserve level is determined to be £1.3m. Earmarked reserves at 31 March 2027 are estimated at £1.962m, but the forecast shows general fund balance going negative in 2027/28 (£1,603m deficit), 2028/29 (£3,264m deficit) and 2029/30 (£3,857m deficit) without delivery of the recovery plan and further EFS.
findings.matters: Negative reserves indicate insolvency. The council cannot sustain operations without continued government support or dramatic operational changes.
findings.figures: Minimum prudent reserves £1.3m; forecast 2027/28 general fund balance minus £1,603m; 2028/29 minus £3,264m; 2029/30 minus £3,857m
findings.quote: the forecast of usable unrestricted Earmarked Revenue Reserves and the General Fund balance over the period 2025/26 to 2030/31...demonstrates that the Council is not financially sustainable in the medium term

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: Recovery plan and governance arrangements still under development and not yet approved
findings.detail: The EFS approval is conditional on delivering a recovery plan including asset disposals and £1m+ in savings/income improvements. However, governance arrangements for the recovery plan were still awaiting approval at the time of this report. The Council set up a 'Recovery Command and Control' group using emergency planning protocols, treating the situation as if a Section 114 Notice had been issued.
findings.matters: Conditions on government support have not yet been operationalised. Failure to establish effective governance risks non-delivery and triggering further intervention.
findings.figures: Recovery plan requires £1m savings/income 2026/27, further £1m for 2027/28; £15.5m EFS conditional on recovery plan delivery
findings.quote: Governance arrangements for delivery of the Council's Recovery Plan needs to be approved to ensure this can be demonstrated to the MHCLG now EFS has been approved

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: Forced service closures and reductions to fund deficit
findings.detail: The council is ceasing operation of Blackfriars Priory from May 2026, reducing museum opening hours from 6 to 4 days, cutting festivals and events support, reducing staffing, and changing community safety management. These are described as part of 'review of Council's discretionary spend' totalling £377k in savings.
findings.matters: Service cuts indicate the scale of fiscal pressure and reduced capacity to respond to new demands or invest in service improvements.
findings.figures: £377k savings from service reductions; total recovery plan requires £1m savings in 2026/27 and further £1m in 2027/28
findings.quote: Cease to operate Blackfriars Priory from May 2026; Keep the Museum of Gloucester Open but reduce its opening hours from April 2026 from 6 to 4 days

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: External auditors issued three statutory recommendations on finance capacity, accounting timeliness, and monitoring
findings.detail: In October 2025, Ernst & Young issued statutory recommendations under Section 24 of the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014 requiring: urgent review of Finance team capacity and capability; clear timetable for producing accounts (the council failed to meet statutory deadlines); and comprehensive review of in-year financial monitoring. The recommendations were presented to Full Council on 25 November 2025.
findings.matters: Statutory recommendations indicate external auditor concerns about control environment and financial governance. This creates risk of audit qualification and potential government intervention.
findings.figures: Three statutory recommendations issued October 2025; council accounts production delayed beyond statutory deadlines
findings.quote: We recommend that the Council urgently review the Finance team to ensure that there is sufficient capacity and capability to support the breadth of its activities, including the preparation of accurate financial information

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: Commercial property income and bereavement services significantly underperforming budget
findings.detail: Commercial property budgets had to be reduced by £1.777m in mid-year (from £3.317m budgeted to £1.540m actual), indicating serious income shortfalls. Bereavement services are also flagged as an ongoing budgetary challenge. These are identified in the financial monitoring report as key drivers of the £2.5m projected overspend.
findings.matters: Income shortfalls on assets indicate either market challenges in the council's area or asset management issues. This affects debt serviceability.
findings.figures: Commercial property adverse variance £1,777k; combined income service pressures a key factor in £2.5m 2025/26 overspend
findings.quote: ongoing budgetary challenges for the Council's commercial properties income, bereavement services income, IT spending, waste spending, and housing subsidy budgets

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: Pattern of serious annual overspends indicating systemic budget management failure
findings.detail: The council has overspent significantly for multiple consecutive years: 2022/23 (£725k), 2023/24 (£826k), 2024/25 (£4.3m), and 2025/26 (forecast £2.5m). In 2025/26, budgets had to be revised mid-year adding £2.845m to the net budget because budgets were set at 'unrealistic levels'. The Section 151 Officer cites 'lack of financial data, lack of engagement with budget officers and limited budget monitoring' as causes.
findings.matters: This demonstrates systemic failure in financial controls, not one-off issues. External auditors issued three statutory recommendations specifically addressing capacity, monitoring, and accounts production.
findings.figures: 2025/26 mid-year budget revision added £2,845k; year-end forecast overspend £2.519m; commercial property had £1,777k adverse variance from budget
findings.quote: some key service budgets were set at unrealistic levels for a number of years through a combination of lack of financial data, lack of engagement with budget officers and limited budget monitoring

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: High short-term borrowing exposure to interest rate risk of approximately £122m
findings.detail: The council has a significant amount of short-term borrowing estimated at around £122m, which creates high sensitivity to interest rate changes. The Section 151 Officer notes that base rates reducing slower than expected has already had direct negative impact. The strategy going forward is to work with treasury advisors to mitigate this risk 'if affordable', suggesting limited capacity to refinance.
findings.matters: Even small interest rate movements could materially worsen the council's revenue position. This is identified as an active risk that may not be manageable given budget pressures.
findings.figures: Approximately £122m short-term borrowing; Bank of England base rate 3.75% in December 2025
findings.quote: A significant amount of the Council s borrowing approximately £122m is short term which leaves a high risk of exposure to interest rate changes

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: 2026/27 budget entirely dependent on one-off government support with no sustainable funding plan for 2027/28
findings.detail: The £9.050m EFS for 2026/27 is a one-off capitalisation direction that 'defers the budget pressure into 2027/28'. The council forecasts deficits of £4.3m in 2027/28 and general fund balances going negative from 2028/29 onwards. The Section 151 Officer states the council 'is currently unable to demonstrate Financial Sustainability over the medium term' and that 'further EFS will be required in 2027/28' if the recovery plan is not delivered.
findings.matters: The council faces a structural funding gap that extends beyond the current support package. Future borrowing capacity and creditworthiness are at serious risk.
findings.figures: 2027/28 deficit forecast £4,316k; 2028/29 negative balance of £2,905m; 2029/30 negative balance of £3,857m
findings.quote: The Council is currently unable to demonstrate Financial Sustainability over the medium term. If this is not delivered it is likely that further EFS will be required in 2027/28

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: Council received emergency government funding to avoid insolvency notice
findings.detail: Gloucester was in a Section 114 position (negative reserves) in 2024/25 with a £4.3m overspend. The council applied for Exceptional Financial Support in December 2025 and received approval on 23 February 2026 for a £15.5m capitalisation direction spanning three years. Without this, the council would have been unable to set a lawful budget and would have been required to issue a Section 114 Notice.
findings.matters: This is a direct indicator of severe financial distress. The council was technically insolvent and dependent on government bailout to function.
findings.quote: without EFS this Council would have been in Section 114

findings.headline: Previous years' overspends and budget resets indicate historical budget management failures
findings.detail: The council acknowledges it is 'facing significant financial pressures due to previous years overspends' and the current plan 'includes the financial impact of the previous year's overspends, the budget reset in 25-26'. This is not a one-off pressure from external events but a pattern: the council's budgets have been wrong for multiple years. The 2025/26 opening balance is stated as zero (adjusted for a £3.89m EFS contribution), indicating the council was cash-generative only through emergency support.
findings.matters: Historical budget mismanagement is a warning sign for future reliability. If a council has consistently overspent its budget for multiple years, that suggests either forecasting is poor or spending control is weak. The current 'balanced' budget achieved only through emergency support and asset disposals inherits this risk.
findings.figures: 2025/26 opening balance: £0 (adjusted from negative position with £3.89m EFS contribution to General Fund balances); 2025/26 budget deficit before EFS: £2.270m
