findings.quote: The Council is facing significant financial pressures due to previous years overspends. It explains what the Council is doing to address those pressures and achieve a sustainable medium-term budget including by delivering the initiatives/actions detailed in the recovery plan.

findings.headline: Council identifies lack of finance and property team capacity as critical constraint on recovery plan delivery
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer explicitly states that 'sufficient capacity needs to be in place for the Council's finance and property teams' to deliver the recovery plan, and this is conditional language: the budget is only 'robust' if this condition is met. The council's own risk assessment identifies 'Finance Team and Asset Management Team capacity and capability' as a risk, with no residual risk score provided (suggesting it may be unmitigated). This suggests the council is already stretched and cannot reliably execute the asset disposal plan or other recovery initiatives.
findings.matters: Even if the council has a good plan on paper, its ability to execute complex asset disposals and service reductions depends on having adequate staff. Understaffed finance teams make implementation errors, miss deadlines, and slow delivery. This is a deliverability constraint.
findings.figures: Recovery plan and budget robustness conditional on adequate finance and property team capacity; Finance/Asset Management team capacity identified as risk factor in 19.3
findings.quote: To deliver the plan, sufficient capacity needs to be in place for the Council's finance and property teams, and governance arrangements need to robust and clear.

findings.headline: £1.297m annual revenue cost for EFS borrowing built into budget indefinitely
findings.detail: The council must service the £15.5m EFS as revenue borrowing, with costs of £1,297k per year shown consistently across all five years of the plan (2026/27 through 2030/31). This is a structural revenue cost that does not diminish. If the recovery plan asset disposal targets are not met, this borrowing persists and consumes revenue funding that could otherwise fund services or be returned to reserves.
findings.matters: This represents a permanent structural claim on revenue: over the five-year plan, £6.485m will be spent servicing this one emergency loan. The council is paying interest on money it couldn't afford in the first place.
findings.quote: Cost of EFS Borrowing 1,297 [per year]. A Capitalisation Direction is funded by the Council borrowing or use of Capital Receipts (e.g. from disposal of assets) which makes delivery of the recovery plan essential

findings.headline: Negative fund balances forecast from 2027/28 onwards, extending through the five-year plan
findings.detail: Despite EFS approval, the General Fund balance turns negative from 2027/28 (£-1,603k) and deteriorates further to £-4,311k by 2030/31. The council explicitly states 'The Money Plan presents negative balances from 2027/28' and acknowledges this 'indicates that the current recovery plan will require phase two initiatives to achieve further reductions to the base budget.' This shows the council's own financial projections indicate the recovery plan will not be sufficient to stabilise finances.
findings.matters: Negative reserves mean the council is operating at a structural loss. Each year it runs a cash deficit that must be covered by reserves or further borrowing. This is unsustainable and suggests the council will run out of cash.
findings.quote: The Money Plan presents negative balances from 2027/28, but this includes the borrowing costs for the £15.5m from 1 April 2026. The draft recovery plan submitted as part of the EFS application sets out an Asset Disposal Plan, generating sufficient capital receipts which, if EFS is granted, may be used to temporarily support the cost of revenue spending

findings.headline: 2026/27 budget balanced only through £15.5m exceptional government support, conditional on recovery plan delivery
findings.detail: The council cannot set a balanced budget without in-principle Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from MHCLG for a capitalisation directive of up to £15.5m. The Section 151 Officer confirms that this sum is 'required to enable a legally, robust and Balanced Budget to be set and to avoid a Section 151 notice being required in relation to 2026/27'. The budget is contingent on MHCLG acceptance of terms and delivery of the recovery plan.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council cannot balance its budget from its own resources and is entirely dependent on government emergency support. A Section 151 notice would be a formal statement that the council cannot set a balanced budget.
findings.figures: £15.5m capitalisation directive covering 2024/25, 2025/26 and 2026/27
findings.quote: a balanced budget for 2026-27 was only achievable due to the in principle agreement by the MHCLG for Exceptional Financial Support for a capitalisation directive of up to £15.5m

findings.headline: Ongoing impact of December 2021 cyber-attack rendered council unable to demonstrate ability to monitor deployment of resources
findings.detail: The 2021 cyber-attack disabled the council's financial systems from December 2021 to February 2023, during which the council maintained only manual records. From March 2023 to April 2024 a hybrid manual-and-system process was used. Throughout this period and beyond, the council was unable to demonstrate the ability to appropriately monitor the deployment of its resources in pursuit of its objectives.
findings.matters: Inability to monitor resource deployment for extended periods is a critical governance and control failure that enabled financial problems to go undetected.
findings.figures: Systems down December 2021 to February 2023; hybrid process March 2023 to April 2024
findings.quote: the attack rendered the Council's financial systems unavailable from 20 December 2021 to 28 February 2023, after which the Council operated a hybrid manual-and-system process from 1 March 2023 to 18 April 2024. During and following this period the Council has been significantly impacted with its servers rendering the Council's system inaccessible as a consequence, the Council was unable to demonstrate the ability to appropriately monitor the deployment of its resources in pursuit of its objectives.

findings.headline: Annual Governance Statement does not disclose known significant weaknesses in financial reporting and internal controls
findings.detail: The council's draft 2023/24 Annual Governance Statement (AGS) does not reflect known significant weaknesses in financial reporting or internal control arrangements. Management and the Audit Committee failed to consider or disclose the implications of identified key control failures, including that bank reconciliations were not up to date and internal audit had to defer reviews.
findings.matters: When a council fails to disclose known control weaknesses in its governance statement, it misleads stakeholders about the reliability of its financial management and loses transparency.
findings.figures: Known weaknesses in control environment not disclosed in AGS
findings.quote: The Council's draft 2023/24 AGS does not reflect the known significant weaknesses in financial reporting or internal control arrangements. In preparing and considering the AGS management and the Audit and Governance Committee should have considered implications of the fact that Internal Audit identified that key control account reconciliations, including bank reconciliations were not up to date

findings.headline: Finance team lacks sufficient capacity and capability to prepare financial statements to required standard and timetable
findings.detail: The council has a recent history of late financial statements (2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25 all late). The core cause is insufficient capacity and capability within the finance team. This chronic weakness has prevented timely, accurate financial reporting and has contributed to control failures and misstatements in the accounts.
findings.matters: Without adequate finance team capacity and capability, councils cannot produce timely, accurate financial information needed for statutory reporting, audit, and informed decision-making.
findings.figures: Four consecutive years of late accounts (2021/22 through 2024/25); 16 months late for 2023/24
findings.quote: The Council has a recent history of not preparing its financial statements in accordance with the statutory publication deadlines with 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25 accounts being late. This is primarily due to insufficient capacity and capability within the finance team

findings.headline: 2023/24 internal audit plan, as directed by management, failed to adequately cover key financial system risks
findings.detail: Management directed internal audit to defer reviews of areas with known control risks. As a result, fundamental weaknesses in the internal control framework were not identified or reported. Internal audit did not provide the assurance over financial controls that it should have.
findings.matters: When management restricts internal audit scope to avoid detection of known weaknesses, the council loses its primary internal safeguard against financial and governance failures.
findings.figures: Multiple audit areas deferred due to data recovery issues
findings.quote: the 2023/24 Internal Audit plan which Management directed did not adequately ensure there was appropriate coverage of key financial system risks at the Council. Management instructed internal audit to defer their review of these areas

findings.headline: Council did not operate fundamental internal controls including monthly bank reconciliations and control account reconciliations during 2023/24
findings.detail: Critical financial controls were absent: monthly bank reconciliations and control account reconciliations were not completed during 2023/24. The responsible Section 151 Officer did not fully discharge their responsibility to maintain an effective system of internal controls. This was partly a legacy of the 2021 cyber-attack but also represents a governance failure to restore these controls.
findings.matters: Absence of basic reconciliation controls creates high risk of undetected error and fraud, and indicates breakdown in financial oversight fundamental to any creditworthy organisation.
findings.figures: No monthly bank reconciliations; no monthly control account reconciliations during 2023/24
findings.quote: the Council did not operate a number of fundamental internal controls during 2023/24 including monthly control account reconciliations and the preparation of monthly bank reconciliations

findings.headline: Effective budget monitoring controls did not exist in 2023/24, preventing timely identification of emerging overspends
findings.detail: The council had no effective budget monitoring processes in place, meaning areas of overspend were not identified in a timely manner. This lack of control prevented the council from promptly identifying, challenging and responding to emerging financial pressures. The underlying 2023/24 budget was also based on incorrect assumptions that were rolled forward without updating.
findings.matters: Without effective budget monitoring, councils cannot manage resources responsibly or detect financial problems early enough to implement mitigating action, leading to larger deficits.
findings.figures: Budget set on incorrect assumptions; £0.826 million actual overspend not caught until accounts closure
findings.quote: the Council did not have in place effective budget monitoring processes, to enable it to identify areas of overspend in a timely basis thereby adversely limiting its ability to identify, challenge, and respond to emerging financial pressures with the implementation of appropriate mitigating action in a timely manner.

findings.headline: Disclaimed audit opinions issued for 2023/24 and anticipated for 2024/25 due to late financial statement publication
findings.detail: A disclaimed opinion was issued on 27 January 2025 for 2023/24 accounts due to delayed publication (16 months late). The 2024/25 accounts have still not been published at the date of this February 2026 report, making a disclaimed opinion inevitable for that year too. This means the auditors cannot provide assurance that the financial statements are free from material misstatement.
findings.matters: Disclaimed audit opinions eliminate auditor assurance and are a severe governance red flag indicating financial reporting breakdowns that prevent effective accountability and decision-making.
findings.figures: 2023/24 accounts published 8 September 2025 (statutory date was 31 May 2024, 16 months late); 2024/25 accounts still unpublished as of February 2026
findings.quote: The Council published the draft unaudited financial statements on 8 September 2025, sixteen months after the statutory publication date of 31 May 2024. We were therefore not in a position to undertake any audit procedures or to start rebuilding assurance ahead of the backstop date of 28 February 2025.

findings.headline: Council has negative general fund reserves of £3.89 million and applied for emergency government funding
findings.detail: After overspending £0.826 million in 2023/24, reserves fell from £4.975 million to £3.099 million. Overspends of £4.3 million in 2024/25 and forecast £2.5 million in 2025/26 have left the council unable to set a balanced budget. The council has applied for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from government to bridge funding gaps while establishing cost reduction and income increase plans.
findings.matters: A council with negative reserves and requiring emergency government funding is an extreme credit risk for lenders and indicates fundamental financial instability.
findings.figures: £3.89 million negative reserves for 2024/25; £4.3 million overspend 2024/25; £2.5 million forecast overspend 2025/26; £0.826 million overspend 2023/24
findings.quote: the Council is unable to set a balanced budget and has applied for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from the Government to address the budget gaps which it faces while it establishes plans to achieve reductions in expenditure and increases income in order to balance the Council's financial position

findings.headline: Cemeteries and Crematorium service income underperforming by £496k due to structural decline
findings.detail: Income from cremations and related services has declined because of a trend towards direct cremations rather than full cremations, reducing wake bookings. This is a structural demand change, not temporary.
findings.matters: A £496k structural revenue loss from changed consumer behaviour indicates permanently reduced capacity in this income stream.
findings.figures: £496k shortfall in income
findings.quote: Cemeteries and Crematorium service income is underperforming to budget by £496k. This trend has been clear over a few years in part due to more direct cremations to be taking place, which is leading to a resultant reduction in the demand for full cremations.

findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio income down by £1.8m
findings.detail: The council's commercial property income is now forecast at £1.5m net, a reduction of £1.8m. Much of the estate is retail-based and affected by city centre regeneration completion and historic portfolio recovery slowness.
findings.matters: Commercial property is a significant income source; the £1.8m reduction and regeneration completion risk create revenue volatility that could affect debt service capacity.
findings.figures: £1.5m forecast income; £1.8m reduction from budget
findings.quote: Commercial Property portfolio is now forecast to contribute a net income to the Council of over £1.5m, a reduction of £1.8m.

findings.headline: £2.8m budget increase in 2025-26 due to unrealistic baseline budgets set for years
findings.detail: Service budgets have been set at unrealistic levels for years due to lack of financial data, poor engagement between finance and budget holders, and limited budget monitoring. This is why the revised budget requires a £2.8m increase.
findings.matters: This reveals systemic budget-setting failures that explain prior overspends and indicate ongoing budget volatility risk; budgets still may not reflect true costs.
findings.figures: £2.8m (£2.845m) increase in net budget requirement
findings.quote: some key service budgets have been set at unrealistic levels for a number of years through a combination of lack of financial data, lack of engagement between finance team and budget holding officers and limited budget monitoring

findings.headline: Council has failed to publish statutory accounts on time for four years
findings.detail: Since the December 2021 cyber attack, the council has not met statutory deadlines for publishing Annual Statements of Accounts. Accounts for 2021-22, 2022-23, and 2023-24 were eventually published in late 2024 and 2025.
findings.matters: Failure to publish accounts on time indicates governance breakdown and prevents creditors, auditors, and lenders from understanding the council's true financial position in a timely way.
findings.figures: 4 years of missed deadlines; accounts for 2021-22, 2022-23, 2023-24 eventually published
findings.quote: This Council has not met the statutory deadlines for publishing its Annual Statement of Accounts since the cyber attack in December 2021.

findings.headline: External auditors issued Statutory Recommendations notice in October 2025
findings.detail: This formal notice was issued by external auditors and approved by Council in November 2025. It indicates governance and financial control failures serious enough to warrant statutory intervention.
findings.matters: Statutory Recommendations indicate formal audit concerns about the council's governance and financial management; they typically precede more severe intervention if not addressed.
findings.figures: October 2025
findings.quote: In October 2025 the External Auditors issued a Statutory Recommendations notice; these, along with the Council's response, were approved by Members unanimously at Council on 25th November.

findings.headline: 2026-27 budget can only be delivered with Exceptional Financial Support from government
findings.detail: The council has explicitly stated it cannot balance its 2026-27 budget without EFS. This dependency will continue into the forward plan and indicates the council cannot sustain itself on its own revenues.
findings.matters: Dependency on government bailout is the strongest signal of financial distress; lenders cannot rely on repayment without explicit central guarantee.
findings.figures: 2026-27 budget undeliverable without EFS
findings.quote: the 2026-27 budget can only be delivered with EFS

findings.headline: General fund reserves are in negative balance
findings.detail: The council's 2024-25 draft accounts show an overspend of £4.3m that pushed general fund reserves into negative territory. This represents a fundamental breach of prudent financial reserves policy and indicates the council cannot meet unexpected demands without external support.
findings.matters: Negative reserves mean the council is technically insolvent and unable to manage financial volatility—a critical risk for lenders assessing repayment capacity.
findings.figures: £4.3m overspend; negative general fund reserves
findings.quote: This level of overspend took the general fund reserves into a negative position.

findings.paper_title: Kings Quarter Phase 2 - KQ Hotel Management Company No2 Ltd Mobilisation Loan Agreement
findings.headline: Council is capturing a £982k spread by borrowing at 5.54% and lending at 7.25%, betting on sustained operational performance
findings.detail: The council borrows from PWLB at 5.54%, lends to the hotel management company at 3.5% over base rate (currently 7.25%), and expects to net £982,207 in interest return over 20 years. This spread depends on the hotel management company being able to service its loan obligations — if performance falters, this return is at risk.
findings.matters: The council is treating this as a financial asset generating return, but the return is contingent on a trading business succeeding. In a downturn, the council would be carrying the debt cost whilst losing the expected return.
findings.figures: PWLB rate 5.54%; hotel company rate 7.25% (3.5% over base); expected net interest return of £3.698m less £2.717m = £982,207 over 20 years
findings.quote: The differential between the Council's borrowing cost and the loan extended to the Management Company is £982,207, which is an additional return to the Council.

findings.paper_title: Kings Quarter Phase 2 - KQ Hotel Management Company No2 Ltd Mobilisation Loan Agreement
findings.headline: Expected rental income and dividend distributions are deferred to 2027/28 or later, creating early cash flow gap
findings.detail: The lease includes a two-year rent-free period expiring in 2026, followed by an additional one-year rent-free period, meaning base rent of £500k per annum does not commence until 2027/28. Dividend distributions are expected only after loan obligations are discharged and the management company demonstrates financial stability — not anticipated before 2027/28.
findings.matters: The council is borrowing now but will not receive rent or dividend income for over 18 months. If the hotel's operations are weaker than forecast, the council will be carrying this risk and carrying costs with no offsetting revenue.
findings.figures: £500k per annum base rent from 2027/28; no rent payments expected until then
findings.quote: the first rent instalments scheduled to commence in the 2027/28 financial year, in line with the Commercial Revenue Plan. Dividend payments to the City Council will only commence once loan obligations have been fully discharged and the Management Company demonstrates sustained financial stability. These provisions are expected to deliver a consistent medium- to long-term income stream

findings.paper_title: Kings Quarter Phase 2 - KQ Hotel Management Company No2 Ltd Mobilisation Loan Agreement
findings.headline: Council bears ultimate responsibility for hotel's commercial success and must take over operations if management company fails
findings.detail: The council retains ownership of the asset and assumes trading risk. If the management company fails, the lease reverts to the council, which would then be forced to directly employ all staff and manage operational matters with IHG. This creates an open-ended contingent liability on the council's balance sheet.
findings.matters: This is material unquantified operational and financial risk. If the hotel does not trade profitably, the council cannot step back — it must either absorb losses directly or find capital to close the operation, both of which could worsen an already stretched financial position.
findings.figures: £4 million loan; hotel is expected to employ over 60 staff directly
findings.quote: Gloucester City Council bears ultimate responsibility for the commercial success of the hotel as per The Forum Phase 2 Cabinet report 15 June 2022. Financial failure of the KQ Hotel management company could result in the Lease reverting to the Council who would then have to directly employ all the staff and become involved in assisting IHG Hotel group for operational matters.

findings.paper_title: Kings Quarter Phase 2 - KQ Hotel Management Company No2 Ltd Mobilisation Loan Agreement
findings.headline: Council is borrowing whilst in Exceptional Financial Support due to negative reserves
findings.detail: The council reported in December that it has sought Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) to address negative reserves and current financial challenges. Despite this position, it is now approving a £4 million borrowing from PWLB at 5.54% to fund the hotel loan. The council states this borrowing requirement was part of the original business plan and does not impede PWLB eligibility, but the timing — whilst in EFS — is material context.
findings.matters: A council in financial difficulty taking on new borrowing and trading risk is a significant consideration for lenders assessing creditworthiness, and suggests the council is dependent on this development's success to restore financial position.
findings.figures: £4 million borrowing at 5.54% from PWLB; total repayment obligation of £6,716,580 over 20 years
findings.quote: As reported in December the Council has sought Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) to address its current financial challenges and negative reserves position; however, this does not impede its ability to access borrowing from the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB).

findings.paper_title: External Auditors Ernst & Young – Statutory Recommendations (Report)
findings.headline: Multi-track cost-cutting programme includes restructuring, asset monetisation, and service reductions
findings.detail: Council pursuing parallel cuts across recruitment (reviewing temporary positions, suspending apprenticeships), fees and charges increases, non-essential spend review, operational restructuring (including review of Ubico waste contract scope and housing revenue reduction), and commissioned Asset Management Review to extract higher income from asset portfolio. Car park charges increased from November 2025.
findings.matters: The breadth and simultaneous launch of these initiatives signals material financial distress; asset monetisation and service reduction typically indicate a council under urgent financial pressure.
findings.figures: Car park charges increased from November 2025; multiple workstreams with no specific targets disclosed
findings.quote: Officers are exploring further restructuring options and other operational efficiencies (including the scope of the Ubico contract and further capital actions to reduce housing revenue spend) and income generation opportunities. Officers have commissioned an Asset Management Review to develop a higher income generating profile from its Asset Portfolio.

findings.paper_title: External Auditors Ernst & Young – Statutory Recommendations (Report)
findings.headline: Budget monitoring processes have been 'not consistent and robust since the cyber attack'
findings.detail: Collaborative budget monitoring between finance and budget officers collapsed after cyber attack and remains inadequate. Council appointed interim accountant for three months to rebuild processes. Finance officers now assigned to specific cost centres. Monthly budget monitoring process rolling out starting November figures. Budget monitoring is now standing monthly agenda item.
findings.matters: Weak in-year monitoring means budget variances are not caught promptly; given zero budget slack, any overspend cannot be absorbed and forces mid-year cuts.
findings.figures: Interim accountant for three-month period; rollout planned for November 2025 figures
findings.quote: Collaborative budget monitoring with the Budget officers has not been consistent and robust since the cyber attack, an additional Accountant has been appointed for three months to set up a budget monitoring process that engages with budget officers and Portfolio Holders

findings.paper_title: External Auditors Ernst & Young – Statutory Recommendations (Report)
findings.headline: Finance team capacity and capability insufficient; formal auditor recommendation for urgent structural review
findings.detail: Auditor formally recommends urgent review of finance team structure and capability. Team was forced onto spreadsheet systems during cyber attack recovery and has not recovered full capacity. Council commissioned Local Government Association structural review (commencing 24 November, results due January 2026) and appointed interim accountant for three months to rebuild core processes.
findings.matters: Finance team weakness directly causes missed deadlines and broken budget control; understaffing or under-skilled teams correlate with further financial deterioration.
findings.figures: New Section 151 Officer commenced April 2025; LGA review to commence 24 November 2025; outcomes January 2026; interim accountant for three months
findings.quote: We recommend that the Council urgently review the Finance team to ensure that there is sufficient capacity and capability to support the breadth of its activities, including the preparation of accurate financial information to support informed decision making and to meet statutory reporting obligations.

findings.paper_title: External Auditors Ernst & Young – Statutory Recommendations (Report)
findings.headline: General fund reserves depleted to critical level by multi-year overspends with no buffer for 2026-27 budget
findings.detail: Overspends in 2022-23, 2023-24, and estimated 2024-25 have reduced reserves by £1.5m. Cabinet told in September 2025 that without urgent expenditure cuts and income increases, the council will struggle to deliver a balanced 2026-27 budget. Budget monitoring summary states 'there is no margin for variances' in the coming year.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves eliminate financial flexibility and indicate deteriorating sustainability; a council unable to balance budget without cuts is a material credit risk for lenders.
findings.figures: £1.5m reduction in reserves from overspends across 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25
findings.quote: The estimated impact at this time was a reduction of £1.5m and it was made clear in this report without urgent actions to reduce expenditure and increase income to increase reserves next years budget would be challenging to deliver.

findings.paper_title: External Auditors Ernst & Young – Statutory Recommendations (Report)
findings.headline: Annual accounts publication deadlines missed every year since December 2021 cyber attack
findings.detail: The council has failed to meet statutory account publication deadlines for four consecutive years following a cyber attack that destroyed the finance IT system. 2021-22 accounts published February 2024 (14 months late); 2022-23 published 27 January 2025 (also substantially late). The council faces a 27 February 2026 backstop to deliver 2023-24 audited accounts.
findings.matters: Delayed accounts prevent timely financial transparency to council members and lenders; this pattern over four years suggests systematic finance function failure, not a temporary recovery issue.
findings.figures: Cyber attack December 2021; 2021-22 published February 2024; 2022-23 published 27 January 2025; 27 February 2026 backstop for 2023-24
findings.quote: This Council has not met the statutory deadlines for publishing its Annual Statement of Accounts since the cyber attack in December 2021.

findings.headline: Council borrowing short-term to fund Forum development with refinancing decision deferred until project completion
findings.detail: Gloucester chose to fund the Forum development with short-term borrowing rather than long-term PWLB borrowing. The council acknowledges the Forum is still under construction and will make a decision on permanent funding structure once the asset is complete, meaning the borrowing will be refinanced at that future point.
findings.matters: Capital project funding arrangements matter to lenders. Using short-term borrowing for a long-term asset creates refinancing risk: if rates rise before the project is finished, the eventual refinancing cost will exceed the current short-term costs.
findings.figures: Bank Rate reduced from 5.25% to 4.50% during 2024/25; short-term investment returns averaged 3.70%
findings.quote: The council have taken the decision to borrow short term to fund the Forum development, short-term rates are lower than long term due to the Normal Guilt curve we are experiencing. Once the asset is complete we will make a decision, alongside our advisors, on the best way to structure our borrowing.

findings.headline: £80m property investment fund established with governance safeguards against political interference in commercial decisions
findings.detail: Gloucester has created a Property Investment Board to oversee an £80m property investment fund. The board evaluates acquisitions, makes recommendations to the s151 Officer, and oversees due diligence in accordance with the Property Investment Strategy. The council has delegated authority to the Council Solicitor to conclude transaction documents. The identified risk is that political priorities could dilute commercial considerations around the investment.
findings.matters: £80m represents material borrowing and investment; lenders track how councils govern major capital programmes and whether governance structures can insulate commercial decisions from political pressure
findings.figures: £80m fund
findings.quote: Property Investment Board set up with a defined Terms of Reference to oversee the investment of the £80m fund.

findings.headline: Cyber incident recovery requiring significant capital investment in IT rebuild and security infrastructure
findings.detail: Gloucester experienced a cyber incident and has rebuilt its IT infrastructure in partnership with NCSC and NCC. The council has invested in additional security products including SIEM, endpoint protection, email scanning, and physical security controls, and is accelerating a cloud-first strategy. An investment budget to implement and maintain the rebuild has been approved.
findings.matters: Major cyber incidents represent material operational and governance risk; recovery costs and ongoing security investment affect capital plans and operational resilience
findings.figures: Investment budget approved (specific amount not stated in register)
findings.quote: The rebuild opportunity following the cyber incident has enabled the council to accelerate its cloud first strategy. The investment budget to implement and maintain the rebuild has been agreed
